source.title: Interpretable Reward Model via Sparse Autoencoder
source.authors: Shuyi Zhang; Wei Shi; Sihang Li; Jia-Yi Liao; Tao Liang; Heng-Xing Cai; Xiang Wang

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; some tables and figures are flattened, but the relevant figure is described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests whether SAE features extracted from LLM activations can be interpreted, using feature examples and activation contexts rather than the original toy-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper uses an overcomplete TopK SAE and reports GPT-4o-generated interpretations of features from LLM activations, which bears on V4. Its weight-editing case study reports changes in reward distributions, but that is about SARM reward control rather than whether SAE features are complete or canonical. SAE geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and toy-network superposition are not tested. Benchmark results and cited claims are not rows for these versions.
record.test_reason: The paper uses a pretrained TopK SAE as a component of a reward model (SARM) and reports its own method's performance: benchmark scores, ablations and a weight-edit case study. Its interpretability evidence (RQ1) is a handful of hand-picked features, described by GPT-4o from activating contexts. It reports no rate, no quantitative validation of interpretation quality, and no comparison with neurons or known features. That makes it a showcase of the tool, not a test of whether LLMs contain dictionary-recoverable sparse features (V4) or of any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SARM's SAE gives feature-level attribution and targeted preference manipulation via value-head weight edits. They report SARM-4B with the best RewardBench 2 overall score (73.6) among the compared models. They also acknowledge that unsupervised SAE features are not guaranteed to match human concepts.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a pretrained TopK SAE in a language-model reward model; it does not reproduce the toy-network method or test superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that reward-model benchmark performance varies with SAE layer position; feature dimension and TopK sparsity changes produce comparatively small overall-performance variation. These are benchmark performance sensitivities, not measurements of V4 feature recovery.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected SAE features of a Llama-3-based reward model receive coherent GPT-4o descriptions. Their value-head weight signs match their apparent desirability (e.g., harmful advice is negative, ethical considerations positive).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features integrated into a reward model can be given semantically coherent labels whose learned reward weights align in sign with human preference.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling the value-head weight of the top safety-scored feature shifts rewards rightward on safety-chosen responses. Other pairs remain largely unchanged (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Editing a single SAE-feature weight in a reward model selectively modulates rewards for contexts activating that feature.

record.peer_reviewed: AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (venue stated in metadata); paper text says preprint, under review.
record.problems: Feature interpretations are generated by GPT-4o from activating contexts, with no independent semantic ground truth or reported quantitative validation of interpretation accuracy. The authors state that SAE features are not guaranteed to align with human-desired concepts. Figure 3 reward-distribution results are figure-only in the supplied text, without numerical effect sizes or uncertainty estimates. Some appendix feature/weight identifiers are inconsistent.
record.rows_left_out: RewardBench 2 scores, SAE component ablations, and SAE hyperparameter benchmark scores are omitted because they measure reward-model performance rather than the claim versions' feature geometry or recovery. Cited SAE findings and general architectural assertions are not study results.

untested.parts: No toy networks, interference, sparsity-dependent phase transition or geometry.
No analysis of neuron polysemanticity or capacity competition.
No alternative causes of polysemanticity examined.
No measurement of how features are distributed across neurons. No quantified rate or validation of interpretable SAE features; only selected examples are shown.
No test of completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, or canonicity. The authors note some features may have unclear semantics.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V4 'supports' label were dropped. The paper takes monosemanticity of SAE features as given (citing Templeton, Bricken and others) and uses them as a tool. Its RQ1 evidence is curated examples without quantitative interpretability scoring, even though the prompt asks GPT-4o for a 1–5 monosemanticity score that is never reported. The random-init versus pretrained-SAE ablation (68.4 vs 73.6 overall) measures reward-model performance, not feature recovery.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network test of overlapping directions, interference, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.

Tests SAE-derived feature interpretation on LLM activations in a reward-model setting; does not measure how widely features are distributed across neurons or compare against a dictionary's recovery of independently known features.
Does not establish feature completeness, stability, or canonical status; the paper notes that some SAE features may have unclear or suboptimal semantics.
Represents features as SAE decoder columns with scalar activations, but does not test whether underlying model features are intrinsically one-dimensional.

rows.subject: SARM
rows.stage_stated: reward model trained on preference data
rows.operation_detail: Interpreted SAE features from final-token activations using activating contexts and GPT-4o-generated descriptions.
rows.measure: Reported feature descriptions and their value-head weights.
rows.value: The paper presents Feature 58353 (calculations/programming, +8.01 × 10−4), Feature 60427 (ethical considerations, +7.06 × 10−4), Feature 13950 (derogatory/offensive content, −8.28 × 10−4), and Feature 17289 (harmful actions/advice, −8.77 × 10−4) as interpretable examples.
rows.note: Examples are interpreted by GPT-4o from activating contexts; this is evidence of interpretable SAE-derived features in the tested setup, not an independent validation of feature semantics.
rows.check: Four hand-picked example features with GPT-4o labels and value-head weights. These are selection or showcase values with no baseline, rate or validation, so they cannot show how often an SAE recovers interpretable features. Not a V4 test.

rows.subject: SARM
rows.stage_stated: reward model trained on preference data
rows.operation_detail: Reported additional interpreted SAE feature examples, based on activating contexts.
rows.measure: Reported feature descriptions and their value-head weights.
rows.value: The appendix presents Feature 36785 (guidance/support, +3.60 × 10−4), Feature 57250 (numerical calculations/problem-solving; the surrounding appendix text gives inconsistent feature/weight identifiers), Feature 5500 (general advice; its weight line identifies w36785), Feature 11941 (violence/crime, −5.76 × 10−4), Feature 30565 (instructions for illegal action, −5.46 × 10−4), and Feature 34669 (risk-taking/consequences, −8.85 × 10−4) as examples.
rows.note: The appendix includes inconsistent feature identifiers in some weight lines, so those pairings cannot be confidently assigned.
rows.check: Further appendix showcase examples, so the same selection issue as r1 applies. The 'partial' state was assigned on the wrong basis. The real issue is inconsistent weight labels in the source. Feature 57250's weight line reads w36785 = +3.51e-4 and Feature 5500's reads w36785 = +7.63e-4. The record omits these values.

rows.value: figure only; text describes a clear rightward shift after the weight edit
rows.note: Shows targeted control of SARM reward scores; it does not measure completeness or canonical status of SAE features.
rows.check: This is a test of the study's own method's controllability (a value-head weight edit), not of any version. The result is figure-only and the multiplier is not stated.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Interpreted SAE features reported for SARM in the tested LLM reward-model setting
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports multiple SAE-derived features with coherent descriptions based on activating contexts (r1, r2), supporting the presence of interpretable sparse features recoverable by an SAE in this setting.
